My mom reads my notes (Hi mom 👋), and we could say that her English is rusted to the bone.
So I guess that in order to understand what I write, she probably uses the "Website translation" feature offered by Google.

That got me a bit worried because in my experience, Google's translation tools have been very hit or miss, sometimes giving me exactly what I want other times some bullcrap that doesn't make any sense. And even at the best of times, when the translation is on point, the emotional value and the meaning behind the words gets lost in translation.

It also tries to translate idioms and other language quirks that don't translate literally so it sounds weird as fuck.

To be sure, I tried it myself cause I was curious about the experience my mom is getting, and it turns out that during all this time I've been judging their tool, Google has been cooking.

How social media changed my relationship with life’s ordinary, imperfect joys.

Last Sunday, I was at home, bored and restless, feeling like I was wasting a perfect day with perfect weather. I walked toward downtown, where I usually enjoy the shops, architecture, and cafes while doing my favorite activities: reading and people watching. This is the perfect recipe for me to enjoy life’s little joys —the “resonance” as I recently learned from the book The Story of Your Life.

Hartmut Rosa, who is not the author of the book but is quoted in it, describes it as the ability to be affected by an experience and to appreciate how it affects us. We yearn for resonance, but we cannot summon it on demand. That is exactly what makes it so powerful.

All that wisdom came to me later, though. That Sunday, I was out to chase a little resonance of my own.

Μην κρατάς νεκρά λουλούδια στο σπίτι,

είναι δεμένα με αναμνήσεις.

κάποιου που πλέον αγκαλιάζει τη γη,

είναι ποτισμένα με στιγμές που χάθηκαν.

αυτή η μάζωξη που σε θλίβει.

στους θαλάμους του μυαλού σου.

items.title: Weeknote 47 2026
items.label: Blogs
items.excerpt:
🫧 Open on Bubbles

Life

Unlimited food

I am not sure about other cities, but till 2019 Surat had all-you-can-eat aka unlimited food restaurants everywhere. There was a cold war on who could offer the most dishes. A few joints were advertising up to 100 dishes! You would find pastries, pani puri, pav bhaji, all kinds of chaats, South Indian, Mexican, Chinese food. The list goes on and on.

But the most famous format was as follows:

10-15 starters. This would include cold pastas, salads, etc.

Few variety of garlic bread

3-4 variety of pizzas

Any choice of cold drink: Pepsi, Sprite, Coke, you name it

Brownie plus vanilla ice cream

Everything except the last point was unlimited.

Prices were reasonable. They charged enough that most of the people would never be able to eat enough to get their money's worth. But outliers definitely existed. And you didn't need to be an adult for that. My school group had absolute gluttons, they would sit there for two hours and keep belting food…

items.title: a rant about thanksgiving
items.label: Blogs
items.excerpt:
There are good things, obviously. Getting to see family I only see around the holidays (which itself is mildly concerning), a reason to gather with friends, good food.

Then there are the bad things. It’s rooted in colonialism, for one. Celebrating the landing of white people on a continent that they have no right to (and would quickly steal from the native people), or some half-baked idea that those people joined together with Native Americans to celebrate. Yay America.

As a vegetarian, I mainly object to glorifying the deaths of millions of animals in service to a “holiday.”

Everything becomes about “turkey day.” We gather round and talk about how delicious the animal was, even though it was raised in captivity and died in fear. A turkey’s entire miserable life reduced to one day where family who otherwise don’t get along celebrate the birth of a terrible country.

items.title: Preparing the earth for a persimmon tree
items.label: Q&A
items.excerpt:
I have an enormous aloe plant (about 6 feet tall, 5 feet across) that we are taking out and replacing with a persimmon tree. I'm wondering if there is something we should do between the aloe coming out and the tree going in to prepare the earth to make the tree more likely to succeed.

Given the size of the aloe, I'm expecting that it'll have a pretty big root structure that we won't be able to get access to (there is cement around 1/2 of the planting area). We have chickens and could set them up in the spot to turn over the earth after the aloe comes out. We could add compost, plant a temporary cover crop, just let it rest for a season to give the roots time to decompose, or just put the persimmon tree in right away and hope for the best.

Where I live doesn't hit freezing, but does get a lot of rain in the winter.

Any thoughts on how to prepare the earth for the new tree?

items.title: Kind over right
items.label: Small Web
items.excerpt:
Someone I know is a wonderful example of living the idea that it’s more important to be kind than right. We had an interaction recently where that idea was on full display.

There was an issue that impacted our relationship. She took accountability even when she didn’t fully need to, and she apologized when she could easily have avoided it. The apology was so wholehearted that it enabled us to move forward.

We could have debated how much of the problem came from the circumstances and how much from my own contribution. All of that falls in the realm of being right. She went straight to being kind, and that sped up the whole process. Our relationship got strengthened because of it.

It was an inspiring reminder of how much I still have to learn about living this idea.

items.label: Hobbies and Creative

Published on 20th November 2026 by Ian Mansfield in London News

Trafalgar Square’s Christmas tree is on its way to London after being felled in a forest north of Oslo this morning, accompanied by Norwegian Christmas carols.

The Trafalgar Square Tree tradition is now in its 79th year and is a symbol of gratitude following the Second World War, when King Haakon VII of Norway sought refuge in Britain and the Norwegian government-in-exile was based in London. In recognition of that act, Norway has sent a Christmas tree to London every year since 1947.

This year’s tree grew in the woods at Høgåsen in Sørkedalen, a few miles north of Oslo, and was chosen from a short list of three following a public vote in Oslo. The 21-metre-tall Norwegian spruce (Picea abies) was about 75 years old, and this morning it was felled by the Lord Mayor of Westminster, Cllr Karen Scarborough, along with the Mayor of Oslo, Anne Lindboe.

items.title: Small portion of damaged gutter = replace the entire house's gutters??
items.label: Q&A
items.excerpt:
Part of a tree fell on my parents' roof, damaging a portion of gutter. A gutter installer says that the only right way to fix this is to replace the gutters all the way around the house. Can that possibly be right? Details below.

The tree didn't damage the roofing itself, but it did cause some of the gutter to get a little bent up and detached from the roof. The damaged area happens to include a downspout and occurs at a roof corner. I reckon about 3' to 5' of gutter length on each side of the corner (so maybe 8' total length) is affected.

You struck a deal with a dragon: twenty years of protection for twenty years of dinner service. The island thrives under the beast's watchful eye, as long as the meals keep coming.

Every year, the dragon wakes up hungrier. You roll dice to work your island, harvest ingredients, fuse them into recipes, and cook them down in the Scorchpot — the pot you keep full or end up in. Get the meal right and you prosper. Get it wrong and you're smoke.
